27.0.0.en: 1 Many have sinned for the sake of the goods of this world, and he who seeks riches turns away his eye. 2 Between the joinings of stones a nail is driven, and between selling and buying sin is wedged in. 3 And iniquity shall be crushed together with the wicked. 4 Unless a man holds fast with diligence to the fear of the Lord, his house shall quickly be overthrown.

27.0.1.en: Behind grave sins lies a deviation of thought, especially in commercial work. Some businessmen look for suitable opportunities that bring them more profit while giving up some upright principles.

27.0.2.en: Trade in general is not evil, but if a person practices his trade at the expense of his upright principles for the greatest possible profit, then although his aim is sound, namely to build up his wealth through trade, yet if the person loses the uprightness of his life he sins, even if others among businessmen are accustomed to it.

27.0.3.en: Many have sinned because of obtaining profit, and he who seeks riches turns away his eye [1].

27.1.0.en: A nail is driven between fitting stones, and sin is wedged in between selling and buying [2].

27.2.0.en: He who does not hold fast to the fear of the Lord, his house is quickly overthrown [3].

27.2.1.en: Just as the nail finds a safe, firm place between fitting stones, so the sin of the love of money hides behind some trading operations, and the remedy is to hold fast to the fear of the Lord. It befits the businessman to walk in the fear of the Lord with faithfulness, truthfulness, sincerity and contentment, even if some businessmen are accustomed to a kind of deceit for the sake of gain. "He that buildeth his house with other men's money is like one that gathereth himself stones for the tomb of his burial (or: in a storm)" (see Sir 21:8).

27.3.0.en: 5 When a sieve is shaken, the refuse remains; so the filth of a man remains in his thinking. 6 The potter's vessels are tested in the furnace, and a man is proved by his speech. 7 The tillage of a tree is shown by its fruit; so the thought of a man's heart is shown by his words. 8 Praise no man before he speaks; for this is how men are tested.

27.3.1.en: When the sieve is shaken the filth remains; so the filthiness of a man remains in his thoughts [4].

27.3.2.en: As long as the sieve is still, with wheat or other grain heaped in it, the sand and dust in it do not show; but as soon as it is shaken the grains fall through and the filth remains to be thrown on the dunghill. So man, as long as he is slack in examining his depths and reviewing his aims under the leading of the Holy Spirit, does not perceive his faults, nor present repentance for them.

27.3.3.en: v It remains now to understand what this commandment contains as addressed to the power of the mind. "Take heed to thyself"; I mean that you observe yourself from every side, that the inner sight of your soul be alert to guard yourself, as you pass through the midst of snares; for the enemy has set hidden snares on every side. Watch everything with all care so that you may "be saved as a gazelle from snares, and as a bird from traps (Prov 6:5) [1].

27.3.4.en: v When you are occupied with some sin, be an accuser of yourself (Prov 18:17), and do not wait for others to bring the accusation. In this you become like a righteous man who accuses himself in the first speech he makes in court, or like Job, whom the crowd of the people in the city did not hinder from declaring his offense before all [2].

27.3.5.en: St. Basil the Great v As a man comes out of his mother's womb naked, so also the soul goes out of the body. Some souls go out pure and shining, others stained and degraded, and a third kind defiled with many sins. Therefore the rational soul that loves God, remembering the trials and distresses awaiting after death and meditating on them, lives in righteousness so that it may not be condemned nor subjected to these distresses. But unbelievers do not have such feelings, for they commit sins, making light of what awaits them [3].

27.3.6.en: St. Anthony the Great As the potter's vessels are tested in the furnace, so a man is tested by his arguments [5].

27.3.7.en: The martyr Cyprian, bishop of Carthage, sees that this statement is the basis of the view of St. Paul and of all Christians concerning suffering.

27.3.8.en: v After the shipwreck, after the scourging, and after terrifying torments of the body (2 Cor 11:23-33), the Apostle Paul says that he suffered no harm, but rather benefited from the trial, because indeed he was proved through such terrible sorrow. He says: "There was given to me a thorn in the flesh, the messenger of Satan to buffet me, lest I should be exalted above measure. For this thing I besought the Lord thrice, that it might depart from me. And he said unto me, My grace is sufficient for thee: for my strength is made perfect in weakness" (2 Cor 12:7-10).

27.3.9.en: When weakness or inadequacy or any ruin takes hold of us, then our strength is made perfect. Therefore if our faith is put to the test it stands firm and receives a crown, as it is written: "The furnace proveth the potter's vessels, and the trial of tribulation proves the righteous." This, in brief, is the difference between us and the others who do not know God: in the day of trial they complain and murmur, but the trial does not let us leave the truth that belongs to virtue and faith, but strengthens us by its sufferings [4].

27.3.10.en: The martyr Cyprian, bishop of Carthage v God has authority over us as the potter over the clay, to form from the same material vessels unto honor and vessels unto dishonor. Therefore, as for you who answer God in a spirit of haughtiness, it is enough for you to hear these things [5].

27.4.0.en: Origen v The lion creeps into a hidden ambush to prey upon the righteous, and earthen vessels are tested in the furnace (see Sir 27:5), and the righteous are tested by trials. For in another place it is written: "My son, if thou come to serve the Lord, prepare thy soul for temptation" (see Sir 2:1) [6].

27.5.0.en: St. Jerome This fire, as St. Augustine says, is the fire of trials, which burns the one whose works were earthly, while it purifies the one whose works were according to the Lord's good pleasure, and increases his splendor [7].

27.6.0.en: v Earthen vessels become hard by fire; so the strength of the body of Christ is not consumed by fire like straw but grows harder like earthen vessels, through the fire of the sufferings (of Christ) [8].

27.6.1.en: v The fire tests the quality of each one's work: if his work endures, the work which he built (and it endures if the person is concerned with divine things, how to please the Lord), he receives a reward for his concern; and if it is burned he loses his reward, because he cannot keep what he loves (earthly things), but he himself shall be saved, yet so as by fire (1 Cor 3:15). This last expression means that without the pain of the fire he cannot destroy the pleasures which he loved to build up.

27.7.0.en: v Here it seems to me that we have a fire which these people do not lose, a fire which brings gain to one person and loss to another, and is a test of both. This fire is not the fire which our Lord means when He says to those on His left: "Depart from me, ye cursed, into everlasting fire" (Mt 25:41) [9].

27.7.1.en: St. Augustine St. Augustine distinguishes between one who is tempted and one who falls into temptation. For in the Lord's Prayer, when we ask "lead us not into temptation," we are not asking not to be tempted, but not to enter into it.

27.7.2.en: v The prayer here is not that we may not be tempted, but that we may not enter into temptation. It is like one who passes through a trial by fire: he does not pray that the fire may not touch him, but that he may not perish by the fire, for "the potter's vessels are tested in the furnace, and the righteous in the trial of tribulation" [5]. Joseph was tempted by the enticements of an adulteress, but he did not enter into the temptation (Gen 39:17). Susanna was tempted but she did not enter into the temptation (Dan 13:20, addition). And so many of both sexes, especially Job [10].

27.8.0.en: St. Augustine v After a man among us confesses his fault, he is transformed by his repentance into a change through knowledge, and shows remarkable progress, and so he is tempted by the enemy, and the strength of his soul and the soundness of his purpose are tested. Indeed Scripture says: He who has not been tested is not worthy of trust. No one will reach perfection unless he is first tested by trials [11].

27.9.0.en: Rufinus v The blessed John the Evangelist, who was certainly not less than St. Jacob (son of Isaac) in merits, declares: "If we say that we have no sin, we deceive ourselves, and the truth is not in us" (1 Jn 1:8). Moreover we read in another place: "A just man falleth seven times, and riseth up again" (Prov 24:16). Therefore, since it was not possible for the blessed Jacob to be without light sins, God wished to destroy these small transgressions in this world by the fire of tribulations. In him was fulfilled the word of God by the Holy Spirit: "The potter's vessels are tested in the furnace, and a man is proved by his speech." Moreover, "God scourgeth every son whom he receiveth" (Heb 12:6) and "we must through much tribulation enter into the kingdom of God" (Acts 14:21). Therefore, in order that God might present the holy Jacob as pure gold on the coming day of judgment, He first removed from him every stain of sin, so that the other witness of fire might find nothing in him to burn [12].

27.9.1.en: Father Caesarius, bishop of Arles As the fruit shows how the tree was cultivated, so the thought of a man shows his heart [6].

27.9.2.en: Do not praise a man before he reveals his way of thinking, for by this a man is tested [7].

27.9.3.en: As the tree is known by its fruit, so a man is known by his speech. For speech is the translation of inner feelings and an expression of the hidden things of the heart: "For by speech wisdom shall be known, and learning by the word of the tongue" (see Sir 4:24). Therefore it is not fitting to praise a man without listening to him. Thus Ben Sira sets great value upon silence and speech: through silence a person listens to his depths and finds the opportunity to know himself and to enter into dialogue with God, and in a person's speech there is a translation of his personality.

27.10.0.en: 9 If you pursue righteousness you will overtake it, and put it on as a robe of glory, and dwell with it; and it will keep you forever, and in the day of visitation you will find support. 10 Birds resort to their kind, and truth returns to those who practice it. 11 The lion lies in wait for the prey; so sins lie in wait for those who work iniquity.

27.10.1.en: If you pursue righteousness you will obtain it, and put it on as a glorious robe [8].

27.10.2.en: Ben Sira fears that there may be a conflict between the demands of wisdom and the demands of wealth, so he makes clear the possibility of overcoming this conflict, saying that he who strives to seek wisdom finds it, and even puts it on as a glorious robe [8]. There is no unavoidable conflict between holy righteousness and the practice of trade. The holy God strives toward man and seeks him, and presents to him His righteousness with the crown in His hand, to set it upon him if he responds to Him.

27.10.3.en: As birds gather to their own kind, so truth returns to those who practice it [9].

27.10.4.en: One of the factors that make the conflict between the holy life and trade possible to overcome is the existence of good businessmen, who are not as rare as some suppose. These can gather together to sanctify commercial work, for birds gather to their own kind. So the godly in every work support their brothers in the Lord.

27.11.0.en: The lion lies in wait for its prey; so sin lies in wait for those who work iniquity [10].

27.11.1.en: The Apostle says: "Be sober, be vigilant; because your adversary the devil, as a roaring lion, walketh about, seeking whom he may devour" (1 Pet 5:8).

27.12.0.en: v Is there anything more terrifying than Satan? Yet we find no armor against him except faith, for it is an unseen shield against an unseen enemy, who aims various arrows in the midst of the night at those who are unguarded. But since he is an unseen enemy, we have faith as a mighty instrument, as the Apostle says: "Above all, taking the shield of faith, wherewith ye shall be able to quench all the fiery darts of the wicked" (Eph 6:16). When Satan casts a burning spark of base lust, faith shows the image of judgment, and the mind extinguishes the spark [13].

27.13.0.en: 12 The talk of the godly man is always wisdom, but the fool changes like the moon. 13 Among the foolish watch for the opportunity, and among the wise be constant. 14 The talk of fools is hateful, and their laughter is in the pleasures of sin. 15 The speech of him who swears much makes the hair stand on end, and his quarrel makes one stop the ears. 16 The quarrel of the proud is the shedding of blood, and their abuse is grievous to hear.

27.13.1.en: The talk of the godly man is wise at all times, but the fool changes like the moon [11].

27.13.2.en: The wise godly are marked by their steadfastness in their godliness, their sincerity and truthfulness, and they are counted men of peace; therefore those who work in trade often rest in them and are reassured by their conduct. But as for fools, even if they swear, others do not trust them nor feel secure in dealing with them. Origen sees that the foolish man is like one sick with epilepsy; when the sickness attacks him he becomes like another person, entirely different from what he is.

27.13.3.en: v Epilepsy attacks its victims at various intervals, and when the sick man suffers from it he seems a person entirely different from himself in good health, when the epilepsy is not at work in him. This same disorder you may find in certain souls, those which are thought to be healthy when they are in a state of self-control and the practice of other virtues. But they become at times as though in a state of epilepsy when their passions provoke them. They fall from the state in which they were, and the deceits of this world and the other lusts draw them away (Mk 4:19). Perhaps you would not be wrong in saying of them that they suffer from a spiritual epilepsy, when they fall through "spiritual wickedness in high places" (Eph 6:12).

27.13.4.en: They often become sick at the time when the passions attack their souls, and they fall into the fire (Mt 17:15). As it was said by Hosea that they become adulterers "as an oven heated by the baker" (Hos 7:4). And they fall again into the water (Mt 17:15), when the king of all the dragons brings them down from the ark, where they appeared to breathe freely, and they fell into the depths of the currents of the sea of human life.

27.14.0.en: This interpretation of ours concerning the fool is supported by the one who says in the Book of Wisdom, concerning the traits of the righteous man: "The talk of the godly man is always wisdom," but the fool changes like the moon [14].

27.15.0.en: Origen The fool changes like the moon: St. Augustine says: [The sun signifies the spiritual, and the moon the carnal... The sun is the wise person, and the moon the unwise person... "The wise man endures like the sun, and the fool changes like the moon" [15].] He also sees that the wise man here points to the wisdom of God incarnate, as the Sun of Righteousness, and the fool is Adam fallen into sin.

27.15.1.en: v Note now what we read in Proverbs: "The wise man continues like the sun, but the fool changes like the moon" (see Sir 27:12). Who is the wise man who continues, but the Sun of Righteousness, of whom it was said: "The Sun of Righteousness shall rise upon me" (see Mal 4:2)? But the wicked, upon whom He does not rise, will say weeping on the last day: "The light of righteousness hath not shined unto us... and the sun rose not upon us." For God made the sun visible to bodily eyes, rising on the evil and on the good (Mt 5:45)..

27.16.0.en: Who is the fool who changes like the moon but Adam, "in whom all have sinned" (see Rom 5:12)? Without doubt, when the human mind withdraws from the Sun of Righteousness, I mean from inward contemplation of the unchanging truth, turning all its powers to earthly things, it is struck more and more with blindness to the sight of what is within and of heavenly things. But when it begins to return to the unchanging wisdom, then, to the degree that it draws near to wisdom (God) in holy love, "the outward man perisheth, yet the inward man is renewed day by day" (2 Cor 4:16). Then all the light of its mind which was directed to base aims is turned to lofty aims, that is, it is turned from earthly things so that the person may die more and more to the world, and his life be hid with Christ in God [16].

27.16.1.en: St. Augustine v Our eyes do not always see (the moon) in the fullness of its size: now it represents the perfection of the round disk, and when it wanes and decreases it shows a lack on one side. And when it grows from a crescent to a full moon it is darkened on one side. And when it is pale the other side disappears.

27.17.0.en: Now it is not without a mystical reason that the divine Creator of the universe made the moon appear from time to time in different shapes. It is a dazzling parable of our nature. Nothing is stable in man. Here man rises from nothing to perfection... and suddenly he undergoes gradual decline, and is shattered by continual diminishing. So looking at the moon makes us think of the swiftness of the changes of human affairs, and teaches us not to be proud of the good things of this life, nor to boast of our power, nor to be seduced by passing riches, but to despise our body, which is subject to change, and to care for the soul because its goodness is unchanging [17].

27.18.0.en: v If the moon causes you grief by its diminishing brilliance and its gradual waning, so much the more ought you to be troubled by the soul that has virtue and through negligence destroys its beauty, and does not remain as it was, but is turned about and changed continually through the whims of the mind. Truly Scripture says: "The fool changes like the moon" (see Sir 27:11) [18].

27.18.1.en: St. Basil the Great v If we feel grief when we see the moon become pale, which recovers what it lost and renews itself, how much more if your soul, full of the fruit of virtue, changes often in its purpose and in its directions colored by rashness. This is the extreme of folly and ignorance, for Scripture says: "The fool changes like the moon," but the righteous continues like the sun (Ps 72:5).

27.19.0.en: The moon has no share in foolishness, for it does not change like the fool, but the fool changes like the moon... The moon works for your sake, and submits to the management of God's will... But you take upon yourself change by your own choice... Without understanding you often find joy in it [19].

27.19.1.en: v The wise man is not destroyed by fear, nor changed by power, nor does he boast over good news, nor is he swallowed up by sorrow. Where wisdom is, there is strength of spirit with perseverance and endurance.

27.20.0.en: The wise man is steadfast in soul, and is not tossed about by the change of events. He does not waver like a child, nor is he moved with every wind of doctrine, but remains perfect in Christ, grounded in love, rooted by faith. The wise man will not be idle and has no experience of change of mood of the mind, but shines like the Sun of Righteousness, who shines forth in the kingdom of His Father (Mt 13:34) [20].

27.21.0.en: v The foolish man cannot of himself become a disciple of virtue or persevere in his aim, for the fool changes like the moon [21].

27.22.0.en: St. Ambrose v God dwells in the midst of His saints, and where there is holiness there is the dwelling of God. God gives a dwelling to men in one way, to those who choose the way of one life and persevere in it. Truly the righteous man is steadfast (unchanging), for he takes one decision, and for all time, to live the righteous life. But the sinner, on the contrary, is inconstant: "The wicked is changeable like the moon" (see Sir 27:11) [22].

27.22.1.en: St. Jerome Limit your time among the foolish, and instead spend it among the wise [12].

27.22.2.en: It befits the believer to choose the suitable time to speak with the foolish and listen to them. Indeed he takes care to flee from them when necessary, because their talk is sometimes meaningless, their jesting silly, and their stories stumbling blocks that corrupt the soul of the listeners. "Esteem your relatives as much as you can, and take counsel with the wise. Let your conversation be with the wise, and all your talk in the law of the Most High. Let righteous men be your table companions, and your glory in the fear of the Lord" (see 9:14-16).

27.22.3.en: The talk of fools is hateful, and their laughter is in the pleasures of sin [13].

27.22.4.en: The talk of fools is hateful, especially their talk about God, for they suppose that He in His heavens has no relation to men while they are on their earth. Fools practice their evils in the darkness, supposing that God does not see them and is not concerned with their lives.

27.22.5.en: v The man who supposes that he is not seen by Him who sees all things, and that his transgressions are hidden by the darkness, dwells in the shadows. In vain he reckons that there is no one who watches him, for the eye of the Lord is brighter than the sun, it uncovers all secrets, and lights up all darkness, and enters into the knowledge of the depths of the heart, and pierces the heights and the depths (see Sir 23:19).. Therefore he is found out like a fugitive and a wicked hireling (mercenary), known before he hides himself..

27.23.0.en: He who supposes that he hides his crime falls into a vain hope, utters vain words and not the truth. Truly the talk of fools is hateful (see 27:13), producing not fruits but wailing. For the speech of a fool is like a (heavy) burden on the way (see 21:16). What is sin but a weight? It weighs down the traveler in this world, so that he sinks downward by its weight. He who does not wish to be weighed down, let him look to the Lord who says: "Come unto me, all ye that labour and are heavy laden, and I will give you rest" (Mt 11:28) [23].

27.23.1.en: St. Ambrose Speech full of oaths makes the hair stand on end at last, and quarreling obliges a person to stop his ears [14].

27.23.2.en: He who dares to use the holy and awesome Name without reserve or reverence, his talk makes the hair stand on end.

27.23.3.en: The quarrel of the proud leads to the shedding of blood, and their abuse is grievous to hear [15].

27.23.4.en: It befits us not to dispute with the proud and reckless, nor to insult them, nor to rub against them, and we should use the methods suitable to them and at the suitable time.

27.24.0.en: 17 He who reveals secrets destroys trust, and shall never find a friend for himself. 18 Love your friend, and be faithful to him, 19 but if you reveal his secrets, do not seek him afterward. 20 For he who has destroyed the friendship of his neighbor is as one who has destroyed his enemy. 21 And just as you let a bird go from your hand, so you have let your neighbor go and you will not catch him again. 22 Do not seek him, for he is far off and has fled, like a roe from the snare. 23 A wound can be bound up, and after abuse there is reconciliation, 24 but he who reveals secrets has no hope.

27.24.1.en: He who reveals secrets destroys his credibility, and finds no friend for life [16].

27.24.2.en: It befits a person to be worthy to become a depository of secrets. This requires that he be wise, enjoying spiritual satisfaction and filled with spiritual and social knowledge. For revealing a secret is counted a mark of shame for the one who revealed it. The faithful friend does not reveal secrets even after the death of their owners, but remains faithful to them even after their departure.

27.24.3.en: Love your friend and be faithful to him, but if you reveal his secrets, do not pursue him closely [17].

27.25.0.en: Just as a man destroys his enemy, so you have destroyed the friendship of your neighbor [18].

27.25.1.en: It is difficult for a person to regain the friendship and trust of one whose secret he revealed.

27.26.0.en: And just as you may let a bird go from your hand, so let your neighbor go, and do not catch him again [19].

27.27.0.en: Do not pursue him, for he has gone far away from you, and has fled like a hart from the snare [20].

27.27.1.en: Ben Sira compares the friend who has lost trust in his friend, because he revealed his secret, to the bird that escaped from the hand of the hunter and flew from him so that there is no way to recover it. And like a gazelle that has come out of the snare and gone off without return to the same snare.

27.28.0.en: A wound can be bound up, and abuse can be forgiven, but he who reveals secrets has no hope [21].

27.28.1.en: It is almost impossible for the friend to regain his friendship with one who revealed his secret, and if he returns to him he does not disclose his secret to him any more.

27.29.0.en: 25 He who winks with the eye devises evils, and no one can avoid him. 26 In your presence his mouth is sweet, and he admires your words, but afterward he turns his speech, and out of your words he lays a stumbling block before you. 27 I have hated many things, but nothing like him, and the Lord will hate him.

27.29.1.en: He who winks with his eye plans evil deeds, and there is no one who can avoid him [22].

27.29.2.en: In your presence his speech is sweet, and he admires your words, and afterward he distorts by his speech what you said, and out of your words he troubles you [23].

27.29.3.en: I hate many things, but nothing like him, and the Lord also will hate him [24].

27.29.4.en: The Psalmist speaks of the hypocrite, saying: "The words of his mouth were smoother than butter, but war was in his heart: his words were softer than oil, yet were they drawn swords" (Ps 55:21). This applies to Judas, who betrayed his Master with a kiss.

27.29.5.en: v They approached Him to test Him (Lk 2:19-26), hiding from Him their deceitful aim. They addressed Him with soft words, while they were like fierce beasts in sheep's clothing. Such as these the Psalmist also rebuked, saying: "Their words are softer than oil, yet are they sharpened arrows" [24].

27.30.s.en: 7. Sin bears its fruit in itself

27.30.0.en: 28 He who casts a stone upward casts it on his own head, and a blow struck by deceit wounds the deceiver. 29 He who digs a pit falls into it, and he who sets a snare is caught in it. 30 He who does evil, it rolls back upon him, and he does not know from where it comes upon him. 31 Mockery and reproach belong to the proud, and vengeance lies in wait for them like a lion. 32 Those who rejoice at the fall of the godly are caught in a snare, and pain consumes them before their death. 33 Malice and anger, both are abominations, and the sinful man holds fast to them.

27.30.1.en: He who throws a stone into the air throws it on his own head, and the blow of deceit wounds the deceiver [25].

27.30.2.en: The devil supposed that he was able to be rid of the Lord Christ by crucifying Him, and did not realize that by the Cross the authority of the devil and all his powers was shattered.

27.30.3.en: v Those who delivered Jesus up (to crucifixion) have become forgotten. The high priests no longer exist, and no high priests came after them. The scribes who condemned Him to death, their minds were darkened and their understandings struck with blindness, and they are no longer able to see the meaning of the holy texts.

27.30.4.en: All those who condemned Jesus to death were delivered up to the enemy of Christ. Those who mocked Him in their turn became an object of mockery when the enemies surrounded Jerusalem and its desolation drew near (Lk 21:20). Those who scourged Jesus were themselves scourged, and have continued so until the time of the fullness of the Gentiles comes in (Rom 11:25).

27.30.5.en: Truly he who throws a stone into the air, it falls on his own head [25]. All this happened because of God's unceasing concern for them, and they become among those who are saved from the Gentiles together with the chosen remnant (Rom 11:5). Truly, had God not left a remnant, they would have become like Sodom and Gomorrah (Isa 1:9) [25].

27.30.6.en: Origen v It happens at times that when an arrow is aimed at something smooth it rebounds upon the one who shot it, and wounds him who wished to wound (another). In this the words are fulfilled: "He who casts a stone upward casts it on his own head" [25][26].

27.30.7.en: St. Jerome He who digs a pit will fall into it, and he who sets a snare will be caught in it [26].

27.30.8.en: v It is written: "He who digs a pit falls into it"; for though they bind our hands and feet (like the three young men), love has authority to loose us. Note this miracle. Those who bound them, the fire set free. It is as though some persons had been delivered to the servants of their friends, and the servants, because of the friendship of their masters, instead of harming them treated them with all gentleness. So the fire acted when it knew that the three young men were friends: it broke their fetters and freed them, and let them walk, and the fire became a passage for them, falling beneath their feet. Justly were they cast into the fire for the glory of God [27].

27.30.9.en: St. John Chrysostom He who does evils, they roll back upon him, and he does not perceive what strikes him [28] [27].

27.31.0.en: It is told of a godly Christian slave that the rest of the slaves in the palace hated him and planned to kill him; so one of them went and informed against him to the master, who devised a plot to kill him. He ordered him to go early to some people outside the city who kindle a fire, to bring something from them, and he had agreed with them to kill him by throwing him into the fire as soon as he reached them. But the good slave, on his way that morning, heard the bell of the church, so he went there, intending to do the master's errand after the Liturgy. As for the informer, in the morning, some time after the Christian slave had left the palace, he thought of enjoying the sight of the Christian slave in the fire. When he drew near the fire the men fell upon him and hastened to throw him into the fire without verifying his identity and without listening to his protest. When the Liturgy ended and the Christian slave went toward the place where the slaves were, he found a fire that had gone out and found no one of the people, so he returned to apologize to the master, who was astonished at seeing him. And after wearying himself with thought he learned the whole truth of the matter, that it was nothing but an informing, and the informer was punished by dying in place of the one he had informed against; thus God returned the evil upon its doer [29].

27.31.1.en: Mockery and abuse belong to the proud, and vengeance lies in wait for him like a lion [28].

27.31.2.en: Those who rejoice at the fall of the godly are taken in the snare, and pain consumes them before their death [29].

27.31.3.en: Many of the Fathers of the Church, such as St. Macarius the Great, affirm that sin bears its corruption in itself, so the wicked man who is determined on his evil perishes as a natural fruit of evil, certain to corrupt. The wicked man has no need of one to restrain and punish him, but what he does brings him bitterness and death! He drinks from the same cup that he filled for himself, unless he casts the cup away through enjoying fellowship with his Savior, and his earnest striving through the holy will in the Lord.

27.32.0.en: v If you remain concerned with the dust, you will in the end be turned to it. It befits you to change, you must be transformed, you must become heavenly [30].

27.32.1.en: Origen Anger and malice are both hateful, and the sinful man possesses both [30].

27.33.0.en: v "Anger destroys even the wise. A soft answer turneth away wrath: but grievous words stir up anger" (see Prov 15:1). Surely all things depend on our decision, whether to stir up anger or to calm it... "A soft answer turneth away wrath," that is, the way of answering in evident humility and without harshness [31].

27.34.0.en: St. John Chrysostom v Our Lord presented most of His commandments to us by persuasion rather than by commands. Gentle rains moisten the earth and penetrate it, but very heavy rain spoils the surface of the earth and presses upon it so that it is not absorbed. "Grievous words stir up anger" (Prov 15:1), and cause harm. When the harsh word opens a door, anger enters, and harm follows [32].

27.34.1.en: St. Mar Ephrem the Syrian Inspired by Sirach 27

27.35.s.en: Keep me from the corruption and bitterness of sin!

27.35.0.en: v You gave me mind and thought that I might know You and love You.

27.35.1.en: In folly I brought my thoughts down to the dust. Grant me to leave the dust and ashes, and to enjoy meeting Your Holy Spirit, who reveals to me my esteem for You, O Holy One.

27.35.2.en: I return to You that You may sanctify my thoughts in You.

27.35.3.en: I despise the pleasure of sin, and my heart burns with longing for fellowship with You.

27.35.4.en: Let me know that my soul is exceedingly precious in Your eyes!

27.35.5.en: v Let my depths be sifted in the furnace of trials.

27.35.6.en: You reshape them and restore to me Your image.

27.35.7.en: By the fires of trials You destroy all that is dust in me, and plant Your Cross within me.

27.35.8.en: You establish Your Kingdom and shatter all darkness in me!

27.35.9.en: v Grant me to soar toward the heavenly places with Your saints.

27.35.10.en: Let us gather together as birds gather to their own kind.

27.35.11.en: I do not fear the devil who roars to devour me.

27.35.12.en: I take refuge in You, O Lion who came out of the tribe of Judah.

27.35.13.en: The snare of Satan is broken, and by You I escape his nets!

27.35.14.en: v Grant me by Your grace to grow continually, to be enlightened by You, O Sun of Righteousness, and to give light always.

27.35.15.en: I shall not suffer continual change like the moon, but through You become a light to the world!

27.35.16.en: I will stay long with the wise, and flee from the councils of fools!

27.35.17.en: Sanctify my mouth, that it may utter only the truth and know neither the wounding word nor the evil word!

27.35.18.en: Let me not know the quarrels of the proud nor their abuse.

27.35.19.en: v Let me cleave to You, O wonderful Friend.

27.35.20.en: In You I cover the weaknesses of my brothers, and in You I walk faithfully, so that I do not reveal their secrets.

27.35.21.en: v Take from me the garment of deceptive hypocrisy, and grant me to put on Your righteousness, which covers my weaknesses!

27.35.22.en: I will not cast a stone into the air, lest it fall upon my head.

27.35.23.en: Nor dig a pit for anyone, lest I fall into it.

27.35.24.en: I will not harbor evil against anyone, lest it come upon me!

27.35.25.en: I will not rejoice at anyone's falling into the snare, nor be glad at the death of a wicked man!

27.35.26.en: Rather let love settle in my inward parts, in my heart and my mind.

27.35.27.en: Let love flow in my blood toward all mankind!

27.35.28.en: Let me taste the foretaste of heaven, so that I know neither malice nor anger.

27.35.29.en: Set me free from every sin and set free all my brothers, that I may experience the joy of the Spirit with every believer!
